answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Deming wrote it in Out of the Crisis, in chapter 1 — “Chain Reaction: Quality, Productivity, Lower Costs, Capture the Market” — on page 11. Both the W. Edwards Deming Institute ↗ and Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ cite it to the book, and a reader working through the chapter page by page logs it at the same page.

source.excerpt: Defects are not free. Somebody makes them, and gets paid for making them.
trail: The W. Edwards Deming Institute ↗ — the organisation founded in his name in 1993 — publishes the line with a source: Out of the Crisis, 2nd edition, Kindle edition, The MIT Press, page 9.
Wikiquote ↗ lists it under its sourced Out of the Crisis heading at p. 11, not under Misattributed. Libquotes ↗ carries the same p. 11 citation.

An independent reader’s notes on chapter 1 quote it as “Pg 11” ↗, sandwiched between other lines they log at pages 11 and 12 — corroboration from someone reading the physical book rather than copying a quote site.

The book’s MIT Press contents page ↗ shows chapter 1 beginning at page 1 and chapter 2 at page 18, so page 11 sits inside the “Chain Reaction” chapter, exactly where the argument about the cost of rework belongs.
source.excerptNote: In the book the sentence opens a short passage in which Deming works out what a production line’s rework crew actually costs — the point being that repair labour is paid labour, invisible on no ledger. Because Out of the Crisis is still in copyright, we quote only the sentence itself and describe what follows rather than reproducing it.

author.name: W. Edwards Deming
author.heading: Who was W. Edwards Deming?
author.metaLine: 1900–1993 · American statistician, professor and management consultant
author.bio: William Edwards Deming (October 14, 1900 – December 20, 1993) was an American statistician, engineer and management consultant who taught statistics at New York University’s graduate school of business from 1946 until his death, and at Columbia’s business school from 1988. In the summer of 1950 he trained hundreds of Japanese engineers and managers in statistical process control, work that led the Union of Japanese Scientists and Engineers to name the Deming Prize after him. American industry only caught up late: the 1980 NBC documentary If Japan Can… Why Can’t We? made him famous at home, he received the National Medal of Technology in 1987, and the W. Edwards Deming Institute was founded in 1993.

misattribution.heading: This one is real — but check the ones next to it
misattribution.intro: Nothing is stolen here: the sentence is Deming’s, in his own book, on a page anyone can look up. The fact-check runs the other way. Deming is one of the most heavily counterfeited names in management writing, and the lines most often printed beside this one on quote pages are not his at all.

items.scope: “You can’t manage what you can’t measure”
items.why: Routinely pinned on Deming, and sometimes on Peter Drucker. Curious Cat’s Deming pages ↗ call it a misquote and point to page 121 of the same book, where Deming writes that the most important figures a manager needs are unknown or unknowable — and that management must account for them anyway.

items.scope: “In God we trust. All others must bring data.”
items.why: The single entry in the Misattributed section of Deming’s Wikiquote page ↗ — the same page that lists “Defects are not free” among his sourced quotations.

misattribution.truthLine: The test is simple: a real Deming quote comes with a book and a page. This one does — Out of the Crisis, chapter 1, page 11, printed with its citation by the Deming Institute itself ↗.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Most management aphorisms flatter the reader. This one is an accusation, and it is aimed squarely at the accounting. Deming’s argument in chapter 1 of Out of the Crisis is that a defect is not an act of nature or a lapse of attention — it is work, performed on the clock, by someone drawing a wage.

That reframing is the engine of the chapter he called “Chain Reaction”: improve quality and costs fall, because you stop paying twice for the same unit. It is also why the sentence keeps resurfacing in software, healthcare and manufacturing talks — it turns an abstract virtue into a payroll line.
context.detailsSummary: The number that follows, and a note on pagination
detailsBody: The sentences immediately after put a figure on it. Deming describes a manager tallying how much of a production line was doing nothing but rework, then reasons that if correcting a defect costs about what making it cost, roughly 42 per cent of that line’s payroll and burden was going into producing defective items and repairing them — after which the manager improved the processes and rework costs fell sharply inside two months. That continuation is transcribed on Goodreads’ Deming quotes page ↗. We could not open the printed page ourselves to check the figure against the book, so treat the 42 per cent as reported rather than independently confirmed.
Pagination shifts with the edition. The print editions put the line on page 11; the Deming Institute’s own entry ↗ cites page 9 of the MIT Press Kindle edition. Same sentence, different reflow.

sourcesVerified.claim: The W. Edwards Deming Institute publishes the quote verbatim and cites it to Out of the Crisis, 2nd edition, Kindle edition, The MIT Press, page 9.
Wikiquote lists the quote in its sourced 'Out Of The Crisis' section at p. 11, and its only Misattributed entry is 'In God we trust. All others must bring data.'
A reader's page-by-page notes on chapters 1-3 record: Pg 11: "Defects are not free. Somebody makes them, and gets paid for making them." alongside other lines logged at pages 11 and 12.
Libquotes reproduces the quote and cites it to Out Of The Crisis (1982), p. 11.

The fuller passage continues '...On the supposition that it costs as much to correct a defect as to make it in the first place, then 42 percent of his payroll and burden was being spent to make defective items and to repair them...' attributed to Out of the Crisis.

Deming lived October 14, 1900 - December 20, 1993; taught statistics at NYU 1946-1993 and Columbia 1988-1993; trained Japanese engineers June-August 1950; featured in NBC's 1980 'If Japan Can... Why Can't We?'; awarded the National Medal of Technology in 1987; the W. Edwards Deming Institute was founded in 1993; Out of the Crisis was originally published in 1982 as Quality, Productivity, and Competitive Position by the MIT Center for Advanced Engineering and renamed in 1986.
Open Library catalogs the 1986 MIT Center for Advanced Engineering Study edition of Out of the Crisis, xiii + 507 pages, ISBN 0-911379-01-0.
The Internet Archive holds a lending scan of Out of the Crisis (MIT Press, 2000), 507 pages, ISBN 0262541157.
The MIT Press contents page for Out of the Crisis lists chapter 1, 'Chain Reaction: Quality, Productivity, Lower Costs, Capture the Market', beginning at page 1, with chapter 2 beginning at page 18.

'You can't manage what you can't measure' is a misquote of Deming; in Out of the Crisis (p. 121) he wrote that the most important figures for management are unknown or unknowable but must still be accounted for.
